checkpoints: Balances stored in minor units (cents, VND, satoshi) routinely exceed `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 − 1) once an account grows large enough, and JavaScript's `Number` type cannot represent integers beyond that boundary exactly.

Coercing a minor-unit string balance through `Number(...)` before subtracting, as in `Number(truthBalance) - Number(ledgerBalance)`, rounds to the nearest representable double once the value crosses that boundary, producing a computed drift that is off by whole units of currency with no error or warning.

The reconciliation endpoint returns `drift` as a JSON number rather than a string, so even a correctly computed backend value gets re-coerced into floating point a second time by any client that deserializes that field, doubling the exposure to precision loss.

The write path carries an identical defect: `parseAmount` calls `parseFloat(raw)` on a transfer amount, so a large transfer can be rounded before it ever reaches the ledger, corrupting the very entries the reconciliation job is meant to check.

This class of bug is more dangerous than a typical crash because it is completely silent — nothing throws, no assertion fails, and the system just writes a compensating entry with a slightly wrong amount, so the double-entry invariant can drift for weeks before anyone notices.

The fix is to perform every arithmetic step on money — parsing, subtraction, and any derived compensating amount — using `BigInt` instead of `Number`, and to parse with `BigInt(raw)` so that malformed input like `"12.5"` throws instead of being silently truncated.

Every money field must be serialized back out as a JSON string rather than a JSON number, since no numeric JSON representation can survive re-coercion by a downstream consumer without risking the same precision loss.

Correctness should be verified by seeding a drift value above 2^53, asserting that the computed drift and compensating amount are exact to the unit, and asserting that the response body carries those amounts as strings rather than numbers.
